title: Long IRC log with relevant conversations
body:
Involving @creationix, @substack, @thlorenz, and others. Almost all relevant topics touched upon.

```
13:20:38 <Domenic_> creationix: so yeah, streams work all day tomorrow and Sunday.
13:20:54 <Domenic_> I could almost certainly use some help, cuz there's a lot to do
13:21:25 <Domenic_> Your experience implementing js-git on top of your streams is pretty valuable
13:21:52 <Domenic_> Although it needs to be tempered by a desire for performance, which might mean sacrificing on simplicity or purity.
13:22:31 <Domenic_> But I am definitely interested in doing as much via layering of small primitives as is possible
13:23:10 <creationix> yay, I have irc again. It's been a while
13:23:14 <thlorenz> Domenic_: maybe there could be a more low level API to allow optimizing for performance and a higher level one for normal use?
13:23:14 <creationix> ITC on chromebooks generally sucks
13:23:17 <creationix> *IRC
13:23:31 <Domenic_> My current thinking is that promise-returning read() is not the lowest level; a sync read() plus a promise-returning wait() [equivalent to node's on('readable')] seems lowest-level
13:23:54 <creationix> Domenic_, did you see my latest proposal
13:23:54 <creationix> it's somewhat like that
13:24:09 <Domenic_> actually I was thinking sync pop() as the name, then read() could be promise-returning
13:24:17 <Domenic_> creationix: I'm not sure I did, link please :)
13:24:20 <creationix> https://gist.github.com/creationix/6587060
13:24:40 <creationix> dominictarr seems to like it. Also he's started a new thread somewhere. Let me find it.
13:24:46 <thlorenz> Domenic_: pop() would give away implementation details (i.e. its an Array Buffer)
13:25:27 <thlorenz> read() as low level and maybe next() as higher level?
13:25:33 <Domenic_> thlorenz: well it's supposed to invoke array feels. it pops off the internal buffer, and the think popped is no longer in the internal buffer
13:25:37 <Domenic_> thlorenz: that's nice too
13:26:05 <Domenic_> although actually I guess I mean shift() not pop
13:26:15 <Domenic_> whatevs, names not horribly important
13:26:15 <creationix> basically my interface has a .pull() method that tells the underlying stream I'm ready for data, and then it later calls my .ondata handler
13:26:42 <Domenic_> creationix: pull() returns buffer contents?
13:26:53 <creationix> no, pull doesn't return anything
13:27:02 <Domenic_> I keep seeing "return input.pull()" :P
13:27:03 <creationix> except maybe return true if it dispatched the data sync
13:27:11 <creationix> oh, I tend to tail call
13:27:18 <creationix> in hopes tha VMs optimize it
13:27:27 <Domenic_> so ondata is zalgo-ish?
13:27:36 <creationix> zalgo?
13:27:41 <Domenic_> sometimes sync, sometimes async
13:27:54 <creationix> I prefer that in my APIs
13:27:59 <creationix> it's simpler to implement
13:28:04 <creationix> (though harder to consume)
13:28:05 <Domenic_> oh, yeah, that's not really ok :-/
13:28:25 <creationix> but for a W3C spec, I'm find with all data events being on their own tick
13:28:31 <creationix> makes usage a lot simpler
13:28:45 <Domenic_> the inherent conflict, as laid out by isaacs, is that read(cb) is an extra nextTick if data is already available, but much simpler. so some kind of readCurrentBufferSync() + tellMeWhenMoreDataIsHereAlwaysAsync(cb) is what you want
13:29:02 <Domenic_> with the idea that you only ever call tellMeWhen... once readCurrentBufferSync() returns undefined or something
13:29:09 <creationix> the streams2 / go / other platforms way right?
13:29:16 <Domenic_> yeah pretty much
13:29:27 <creationix> right, that's the idea with .pull() returning true if it was sync
13:29:42 <creationix> so you can do while (stream.pull());
13:29:52 <Domenic_> tbh, also, moving away from promise-returning read() helps us differentiate from the existing W3C streams proposal (the one with no backpreessure)
13:30:52 <creationix> so in the streams1 writable API, there was the write return value and the "drain" event
13:30:53 <creationix> we could do the same for readable
13:30:55 <Domenic_> creationix: if you want to open an issue explaining your proposal (with words :P), especially how it compares to read(cb) and readCurrentBufferSync(), that would be helpful. It sounds slightly different, and there's probably something to learn there.
13:30:56 <creationix> read would return undefined if there was no data
13:30:56 <creationix> but otherwise return the data sync
13:30:57 <creationix> and have "readable" event
13:30:59 <creationix> (which actually is basically what streams2 does right)
13:31:08 <Domenic_> yeah that's the idea i think
13:31:32 <creationix> My main goal is to keep confusion out of the bare API
13:31:35 <Domenic_> although promises (or cbs) instead of events makes more sense since you really want a one-time notification to start re-reading
13:31:40 <creationix> but still have the nessecary primitives
13:32:13 <creationix> Domenic_, so in practice, there are cases where callback/promise based read streams are natural and other cases where event handlers are naturan
13:32:15 <creationix> *natural
13:32:27 <Domenic_> right, yeah, passive data listening being the obvious event case
13:32:33 <creationix> hence why node now supports both types
13:32:54 <creationix> and not all streams need backpressure
13:32:56 <Domenic_> isaacs is pretty insistent (as is most of node core) that making EEs part of the stream abstraction was a mistake
13:33:06 <creationix> agreed here
13:33:11 <ogd> for perf reasons yes
13:33:20 <creationix> though I feel the same way about promises
13:33:27 <Domenic_> well if you don't want backpressure I think you'll want something simpler, e.g. a generator of promises or something I think.
13:33:33 <creationix> but is promises were a fast primitive in the language itself, that may be different
13:33:49 <Domenic_> right, that's the decider, is would they be fast enough. i am hopeful.
13:34:00 <creationix> can we use generators in this proposal?
13:34:06 <Domenic_> it would be nice to be able to do `while (data = yield stream.read())` though
13:34:10 <Domenic_> yes definitely
13:34:18 <Domenic_> but it is harder to make use of them than you'd think
13:34:27 <Domenic_> because once a generator is "empty" it can never become un-empty
13:34:29 <creationix> that's the interface I've been pushing for years with lua coroutines and js generators
13:34:30 <thlorenz> Domenic_: but now it's a push again
13:34:40 <Domenic_> thlorenz: ???
13:34:43 <thlorenz> i.e. it'll keep yielding (pushing) values
13:34:46 <Domenic_> so e.g. you can't start out with an empty stream that starts filling with data
13:35:01 <thlorenz> I'd keep read simple
13:35:16 <Domenic_> thlorenz: you have a very weird conception of "pull" vs. "push", but yeah, I remember from yesterday.
13:35:30 <thlorenz> it should by sync and have no (promise, callback, yiedld, future) whatevs API
13:35:34 <Domenic_> thlorenz: to me pull vs. push means "data is buffered until you ask" vs "data is thrown at you and you might miss it"
13:35:50 <thlorenz> that's not how it works
13:36:00 <Domenic_> thlorenz: well it needs to be async at some level, so you know when new data is available to read synchronously
13:36:03 <creationix> Domenic_, not sure I understand the problem?
13:36:05 <thlorenz> push buffers data for you if you don't handle it fast enough
13:36:29 <rowbit> substack, pkrumins: These encoders are STILL down: 50.57.103.135(free2)
13:36:32 <creationix> Domenic_, push can work just fine as long as the stream starts paused
13:36:33 <thlorenz> Domenic_: yes, something to replace on('readable'
13:36:36 <creationix> and it stops emitting data the instant you tell it to pause
13:36:52 <Domenic_> creationix: well a naive model of streams is a generator of promises. but if you ever call .next() before the previous promise is fulfilled, you kill the generator and can't recover.
13:37:08 <creationix> Domenic_, then don't do that?
13:37:17 <creationix> in mine I throw an error if that's done
13:37:24 <creationix> I only allow one read at a time
13:37:41 <Domenic_> creationix: i mean yeah that is part of it. feels fragile though. why use generators at all in that case?
13:37:52 <creationix> right, I don't use generators *in* the stream
13:37:54 <Domenic_> you can't consume with for of
13:38:02 <creationix> I just consume the stream with generators
13:38:09 <Domenic_> what does that look like in code
13:38:14 <creationix> the stream just returns promises from the read
13:38:32 <creationix> while (data = yield stream.read());
13:38:37 <Domenic_> sure ok
13:38:50 <creationix> and yield goes to gen-run or something that resolves the continuable/promise
13:38:56 <Domenic_> i misinterpreted what you meant by "use generators" I guess.
13:38:59 <substack> Domenic_: events should still be part of the stream api
13:39:11 <thlorenz> Domenic_: creationix I stick to my stance that read should never delay - mixing these concepts make things unnec complex
13:39:16 <Domenic_> you seem to have meant "design an API so that it is nice to use when consumers have generators"
13:39:20 <creationix> all of js-git can be used with node style callbacks or continuables
13:39:23 <Domenic_> substack: interesting, why.
13:39:25 <substack> if I'm consuming a stream I want to know when it's done giving me data
13:39:30 <creationix> so you can use generators to consume the streams if you want
13:39:35 <substack> this is one thing I really dislike about the current streams
13:39:50 <substack> even if you're consuming a stream, you have no way from outside to know when it's done
13:39:57 <substack> and that's such a common use-case
13:39:59 <Domenic_> substack: sample use case?
13:40:12 <creationix> substack, that's what the end event is for right?
13:40:14 <substack> a.pipe(b); b.on('end', function () {}) only works if b is in flow mode
13:40:17 <substack> er sorry
13:40:27 <substack> a.pipe(b); a.on('end', function () {}) only works if a is in flow mode
13:40:29 <creationix> oh, pipe right
13:40:38 <substack> creationix: only in flow mode
13:40:39 <Domenic_> hmm
13:40:49 <creationix> when I design stream interfaces I make them simple enough that you don't need pipe
13:40:52 <Domenic_> why do you care when a has no more data
13:40:57 <substack> having good consistent semantics for "hangup" kinds of events would also be really good
13:41:05 <substack> for when the stream gets destroyed
13:41:10 <substack> to unregister listeners
13:41:22 <creationix> js-git streams are readable only and treated like primitive values
13:41:28 <substack> Domenic_: because often I want to do something like this:
13:41:32 <creationix> you write to things by handing a stream to a sink
13:41:45 <substack> a.pipe(fs.createWriteStream('output.txt')); a.on('end', function () { do the next thing... })
13:41:56 <Domenic_> substack: my current plan for that is that the stream constructor gets passed a function to call when the stream is aborted and/or done.
13:42:09 <creationix> substack, with js-git style APIs, you do output.sink(input, callback)
13:42:19 <creationix> where the callback gets called for error or end of stream
13:42:29 <substack> Domenic_: but if I didn't create the stream myself, that doesn't help
13:42:38 <Domenic_> substack: yeah.
13:42:40 <substack> if I got `a` from some existing function for example
13:43:03 <Domenic_> one interface that other languages have I think is a.pipe(b).then(callThisWhenPipingIsOver, callThisIfPipingFails)
13:43:26 <substack> Domenic_: what about having a 'close' event that ALWAYS fires when a stream is "done"
13:43:29 <Domenic_> this output.sink(input) vs. input.pipe(output) thing is curious.
13:43:37 <substack> whether done by being destroyed, ended, or errors
13:43:38 <Domenic_> substack: the problem is that then streams are EEs and isaacs will be sad.
13:44:22 <substack> I think isaacs's "event emitters are always bad in streams" is too broad of a prohibition
13:44:38 <substack> event emitters are really good for hooking up state changes that are immediate
13:44:48 <substack> 'data' and 'end' are not immediate was the problem
13:45:01 <Domenic_> I am tempted to throw more promises at the problem (stream.end.then(noErrors, thereWereErrors)). That is probably slightly better. But kind of silly also.
13:45:06 <substack> but other kinds of events like disconnects and 'close' are
13:45:12 <Domenic_> substack: what do you mean by "immediate"
13:45:31 <substack> events fire immediately
13:45:49 <Domenic_> stream.end promise is pretty useful (eg. you can subscribe after the stream is already over) but still feels weird...
13:45:50 <substack> but data and EOF fire when you read, which is not immediate
13:45:50 <creationix> substack, I'm not sure the stream interface should worry about things like close
13:45:50 <creationix> node conflates too much imho
13:45:57 <creationix> streams should care about "data", "end", "error", backpressure, reading, writing
13:46:09 <substack> Domenic_: will I have to use promises to get at these events :/
13:46:30 <substack> because if so the first thing I am going to do is wrap everything in an event emitter so I don't have to look at them ever
13:46:36 <Domenic_> substack: one-time events which you often want to subscribe to after they've already fired should generally be promises (e.g. document.ready), so yeah.
13:46:47 <Domenic_> substack: that's a shame, feels close-minded of you.
13:46:57 <Domenic_> substack: but if something has real EE semantics then of course it'll be an event emitter
13:47:13 <creationix> substack, just imagine he says callback when you hear promise
13:47:14 <creationix> same behavior
13:47:15 <Domenic_> e.g. if it can occur more than once
13:47:20 <Domenic_> creationix: yes thanks :)
13:47:32 <substack> promises use callbacks
13:47:46 <substack> promises are like forcing everybody to use your wonky flow control library
13:48:01 <substack> instead of the base thing that every async abstraction has in common
13:48:10 <Domenic_> they're like forcing everyone to use weird higher-level primitives like "functions" when everyone has this base abstraction of gotos and labels in common.
13:48:31 <Domenic_> but let's please set aside our differences on this issue ... it's pretty tangential.
13:48:41 <Domenic_> the sematnics are what's important: one-time vs. recurring.
13:48:51 <creationix> like I said, don't focus on callback vs promise vs continuable
13:48:59 <creationix> they are all the same thing from a design point of view
13:49:10 <creationix> I obviously prefer continuables, but whatever
13:49:52 <substack> streams should just have a way of firing some code when they are done being consumed
13:50:13 <substack> because then you can pipe 2 streams together without having had to create them yourself
13:50:17 <Domenic_> +1, that is a big takeaway
13:50:38 <substack> it's very often to pipe 2 things together and then to want to do something else when that finishes
13:50:43 <creationix> substack, so your goal is to know when each piece of a stream chain is done individually?
13:50:50 <substack> whatever isaacs says about EEs always being bad
13:50:50 <Domenic_> substack: what do you think of a.on('done') vs. a.pipe(b, function (err) { ... })
13:51:14 <substack> Domenic_: I think 'done' is cleaner but both would work
13:51:48 <substack> the cb arg might get in the way of other arguments to .pipe() like opts
13:52:01 <substack> like whatever { end: false } is in the w3 streams
13:52:45 <Domenic_> ah wow i totally forgot that w3 streams missed { end: false }
13:52:47 <Domenic_> that's an important one
13:52:52 <Domenic_> should have busted their balls for that
13:52:52 <chrisdickinson> creationix: do your sinks still return continuables?
13:53:18 <Domenic_> BTW everyone: W3C streams = current proposal from those two guys = bad. WHATWG streams = my (our) proposal = good
13:53:21 <chrisdickinson> (would it be possible to phrase "end" as "output.sink(input).then(…)" in promise-land?)
13:53:43 <Domenic_> chrisdickinson: well the promise version would be equivalent to the function (err) { ... } version I did above
13:53:45 <creationix> chrisdickinson, right
13:54:02 <Domenic_> but that's different semantics than the on('done')
13:54:49 <creationix> WHATWG vs W3C, fight!
13:55:48 <Domenic_> (WHATWG = open to anyone, works on real "living standards", CC0, mostly GitHub these days; W3C = pay to play, DRM, copyright, copies and pastes WHATWG standards into their repos and then shoves them through this crazy multi-year editor's draft -> working draft -> etc. -> recommendation process.)
13:56:18 <chrisdickinson> wouldn't returning a promise give the writable streams / sinks / destinations a single point at which to say "I'm done", and "I had an error" or "I was successful"?
13:56:36 <Domenic_> chrisdickinson: not sure, what do you mean more concretely?
13:56:38 <creationix> chrisdickinson, that's what I use the continuables
13:56:46 <creationix> continuable == promise
13:56:48 <chrisdickinson> creationix: right
13:57:20 <creationix> I really, *really* like the idea of treating a stream like a primitive
13:57:25 <chrisdickinson> was seeing if that would be an amenable way to solve the "tell me when this stream is done" problem (vs. making it an eventemitter)
13:57:28 <creationix> transforms accept streams and return new streams
13:57:43 <creationix> sinks accept streams and return promise for "done" or "error"
13:57:45 <chrisdickinson> and was suggesting promises over continuables since that's the way things seem to be moving in the browser.
13:57:53 <chrisdickinson> ok, cool
13:58:04 <Domenic_> creationix: Raynos: why do you guys find the idea of sink.accept(source) better than source.pipe(sink)
13:58:23 <creationix> Domenic_, because it's less code
13:58:31 <creationix> lesss code == less complexity generally
13:58:33 <Domenic_> creationix: for who
13:58:46 <creationix> everyone
13:59:04 <creationix> dest.sink(source) vs source.pipe(sink) is the same code
13:59:05 <Domenic_> creationix: be more specific then. how?
13:59:19 <creationix> but to implement it, only writable things need to implement sink
13:59:35 <creationix> most the links between a source and a dest are transforms
13:59:41 <creationix> and they have a different interface
13:59:46 <creationix> transform(stream) -> stream
14:00:06 <creationix> where sink is sink(stream) -> promise<end/done>
14:00:10 <Domenic_> i find node's .pipe really ergonomic
14:00:13 <chrisdickinson> anecdotally, using simple-streams (the spec that preceded what creationix linked) was easy to follow, easy to write new transformation streams, and made it easy to encapsulate logic
14:00:55 <creationix> all of js-git is still simple-streams for reference
14:00:55 <creationix> the new idea is still just an idea
14:00:58 <creationix> to try to solve some of the pain points in implementing simple-streams
14:01:00 <creationix> in particular error reporting
14:01:08 <Domenic_> substack: you love pipe, how do you react to all this talk of dest.sink(source) intead of source.pipe(dest), and gzipTransform(source) vs. source.pipe(new GzipTransform)
14:01:11 <creationix> I hate it that I have to wait till the next .read() call to emit an error
14:01:32 <Domenic_> creationix: how do errors get emitted in the new idea?
14:01:34 <creationix> I agree that source.pipe(dest) is more natural
14:01:46 <creationix> in the new idea, part of the stream interface is an error event
14:01:48 <chrisdickinson> what I found I liked best about it was that it was simple enough to write a stream sans any supporting infrastructure -- vs. node streams, which always involve subclassing or using another library to create a base stream for you.
14:01:52 <Domenic_> creationix: would love a promise explanation of the new idea, code is not easy to figure out which parts are profound vs. which are just details.
14:01:59 <Domenic_> s/promise/prose
14:02:03 <Domenic_> (O_o)
14:02:08 <creationix> lol
14:02:27 <creationix> chrisdickinson, yes, that was my main goal!
14:02:32 <Domenic_> hmm yeah
14:02:35 <creationix> simple-streams don't need a library to be usable
14:02:40 <Domenic_> everyone uses through anyway
14:02:45 <creationix> you just create objects that conform to some simple interface
14:02:52 <creationix> I don't
14:02:54 <creationix> :P
14:03:16 <creationix> also remember I'm not node-centric with js-git
14:03:21 <creationix> most my platforms are non-node actually
14:03:31 <Domenic_> the constructor pattern in whatwg/streams seems to help some, i.e. you will have to subclass less and just use the constructor with different onRead functions instead.
14:04:43 <creationix> Domenic_, ok, so lets start with the bare abstract goals
14:04:43 <creationix> 1. we want a data stream with back-pressure
14:04:50 <creationix> 2. we want a way to signal the end of the stream
14:05:00 <creationix> 3. we want a way for the consumer to notify the source it's done consuming (abort)
14:05:07 <creationix> 4. we need sane error reporting
14:05:43 <Domenic_> let me add some others that we need, probably not in the base layer:
14:05:48 <Domenic_> 5. multi-destination pipe
14:05:49 <creationix> so we want readable *and* writable interfaces?
14:05:56 <creationix> or stick with readable only using sinks for writable?
14:06:22 <Domenic_> creationix: definitely want writable. So e.g. <video> tags can implement writable and you can start writing frames to them.
14:06:58 <creationix> for file-streaming situations, I like readable-only
14:07:06 <creationix> not sure about the <video> case, that's gray
14:07:30 <Domenic_> WebWorkers: duplex streams, write data in, read data back out
14:07:46 <creationix> to me a duplex stream is just two streams
14:07:55 <creationix> they can be the same object if the interfaces don't conflict
14:08:03 <creationix> but it's really two streams
14:08:03 <Domenic_> Future awesome world (TM): getXHRStream().pipe(webWorkerToDoComplexProcessing).pipe(videoTagStream)
14:08:15 <Domenic_> creationix: agreed.
14:08:40 <chrisdickinson> .pipe(webglTexture)?
14:08:42 <creationix> as far as multi-destination pipe, I think that's just a custom transform
14:08:51 <creationix> it shouldn't be part of the core stream API
14:09:10 <creationix> unix streams don't have that, you use the tee program
14:09:19 <Domenic_> creationix: as long as that can be done performantly, seems good.
14:09:25 <Domenic_> although the base API will probably have it
14:09:39 <Domenic_> but, implemented in terms of a simpler API + a T stream
14:09:44 <Domenic_> (both of which will be exposed)
14:09:58 <creationix> tee(source, 2) -> [output, output]
14:10:02 <creationix> or something like that
14:10:34 <Domenic_> I really liked what Raynos did at https://github.com/whatwg/streams/issues/1#issuecomment-27545472
14:10:40 <creationix> in js-git I have multiplexers and demultiplexors
14:10:47 <creationix> parse(stream) -> { pack: stream, progress: stream, error: stream, line: stream }
14:10:56 <creationix> encode({streams...}) -> stream
14:11:08 <creationix> all custom connectors
14:11:31 <creationix> oh heh, that's the github link I was looking for
14:11:40 <creationix> I should have remembered you've seen it
14:11:47 — creationix slaps forehead
14:12:41 <creationix> so basically, include some generic helpers as builting
14:12:45 <creationix> *builtins
14:12:47 <creationix> I'm find with that
14:13:03 <creationix> as long as they are truly generic *and* useful
14:13:46 <Domenic_> we are trying to make this as much "extensible web" as possible
14:14:02 <Domenic_> it's a bit tricksy because the community hasn't finished experimenting and settled on something perfect yet
14:14:13 <Domenic_> so we can't just rubber-stamp node streams and say "good to go"
14:14:39 <Domenic_> but we want streams as a low-level primitive, not just a magic part of XHR and a magic part of web filesystem APIs and so on
14:15:20 <Domenic_> and to be most useable by others who are building their own custom streams, yeah, small useful and generic helpers that compose the higher-level API that we want to expose
14:15:57 <creationix> yes
14:15:57 <creationix> since we still haven't found the perfect API, I say we should err on the side of simple
14:16:00 <creationix> better to do too little than too much
14:16:26 <Domenic_> yeah. modulo the fact that we need to actually solve all the problems.
14:16:34 <creationix> pipe in streams1 was unusable for voxer, so they never used it and had a custom pipe
14:16:50 <rowbit> Hourly usage stats: [developer: 5, free: 34]
14:16:54 <creationix> which problems should we optimize for
14:16:59 <Domenic_> would still really like a creationix vs. substack fight on source.pipe(dest) vs. dest.sink(source). maybe with commentary from isaacs.
14:17:21 <creationix> dominictarr likes .pipe too I think
14:17:34 — chrisdickinson too
14:17:39 <creationix> I like it, I just can't justify the complexity it entails to implement
14:17:48 <creationix> I hate APIs that require me to use complex tools
14:18:01 <Domenic_> creationix: all of node's use cases + https://dvcs.w3.org/hg/streams-api/raw-file/tip/Overview.htm#consumers seems like a start.
14:18:15 <chrisdickinson> is it still a matter of `dest.sink(transformC(transformB(transformA(source))))`?
14:18:21 <Domenic_> why is .sink easier to implement than .pipe
14:18:23 <chrisdickinson> (re the `sink` version?)
14:18:57 <creationix> chrisdickinson, that's the simple way, yes
14:19:04 <creationix> pure functional programming
14:19:10 <creationix> parallels map functions
14:19:19 <creationix> var object = JSON.parse(json)
14:19:20 <isaacs> Domenic_: i'm more insistent than that. I maintain that EEs should not be in node *at all*
14:19:35 <Domenic_> creationix: how do transform functions work with non-chunkwise transforms (e.g. gzip)
```
